name: ps
tasks: how long has a process run

examples.does: Every process, with user, CPU and memory
Every process as a tree (who started what)
The processes using the most memory
How long one process has been running

pitfalls: ps aux (no dash) and ps -ef are two styles; both list everything.

name: top
summary: Live view of CPU, memory and processes
tasks: snapshot of top for a ticket

examples.does: Live view. M sorts by memory, P by CPU, 1 shows each CPU, q quits
Start sorted by memory
One snapshot as plain text, e.g. for a ticket

pitfalls: High 'wa' in the CPU line means waiting for disk, not a busy CPU. Check iostat.

examples.does: Live view. F6 sort, F5 tree, F9 send a signal, q quits
Only one user's processes

name: kill
summary: Send a signal to a process (stop it)

examples.does: Ask a process to stop (TERM)
Force it to stop now (KILL, same as kill -9); it cannot clean up
List signal names and numbers

pitfalls: Try plain kill first and wait a few seconds; KILL gives the process no chance to save its work.
For a service, use systemctl stop or restart, or systemd may start it again.

name: pkill
tasks: stop all of a user's processes

examples.does: Stop processes whose full command line matches
Stop every process of one user
Send HUP (many daemons reload their config on it)

pitfalls: Run pgrep with the same pattern first to see what would be hit.

examples.does: IDs and command lines of matching processes
One user's processes, with names
Match anywhere in the full command line

name: nice
summary: Start a command with lower priority
tasks: run a backup without slowing the server

examples.does: Run a heavy job at lower CPU priority

pitfalls: nice affects CPU only. For disk, also use ionice -c 3.

name: renice
summary: Change the priority of a running process
tasks: lower priority of a running process

examples.does: Lower a running process's CPU priority

pitfalls: Only root can raise priority (a negative value).

name: lsof
summary: Which processes have which files and ports open
tasks: which process is using a port
deleted file still using disk space

examples.does: Processes using port 80
Deleted files still held open (their space is not freed yet)
Who has this file open
Every file and socket one process has open
Who is using files under a folder (when umount says busy)

pitfalls: Without sudo you only see your own processes.

name: free

examples.does: Memory and swap in K, M and G
Repeat every 5 seconds (Ctrl-C stops)

pitfalls: Read the 'available' column. Linux uses spare memory for cache, so 'free' is usually small and that is normal.

name: uptime
summary: How long the server has run, and its load

examples.does: Time up, users, and load average over 1, 5 and 15 minutes
The date and time it started

pitfalls: Load average counts processes running or waiting. Compare it with the number of CPUs (nproc).

name: vmstat
summary: CPU, memory, swap and I/O every few seconds

examples.does: 5 lines, one per second. si/so above 0 = swapping; wa = waiting for disk
Wide columns, until Ctrl-C
Memory and event totals as a list

pitfalls: The first line is the average since boot. Read the lines after it.

name: iostat

examples.does: Per-disk load, 3 reports. %util near 100 = the disk is the bottleneck

pitfalls: iostat is in the sysstat package; install it if the command is missing.
The first report is the average since boot.

name: pidstat
summary: CPU, memory and disk use per process, every few seconds

examples.does: Disk reads and writes per process (kB/s), 5 times, one per second
CPU use per process, 5 times, one per second
Memory per process and page faults, 5 times
Disk I/O of one process every 2 seconds, until Ctrl-C

pitfalls: Without sudo, other users' processes may be missing from the list.
It shows only processes that were active during the interval.

name: strace
summary: Watch the system calls a process makes
tasks: which files does a program open

examples.does: Attach to a running process and its threads, with times (Ctrl-C detaches)
Only file opens: shows which files a program reads
Count system calls and time spent in each

pitfalls: strace slows the traced process a lot. Keep it short on production.
